query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a thin nickel layer prior to copper infiltration will improve interfacial wetting and bonding during transient liquid‐phase sintering, thereby reducing phase separation and void formation in W–Cu composites for fusion reactor joint applications.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite starting from tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten regions embedded in a copper matrix produced by conventional methods (e.g., spark-plasma sintering or metal 3D printing) without interfacial modification.
generation.intervention: Apply a uniform, nanometer‐scale nickel coating (e.g., 50–100 nm) on tungsten particles before copper infiltration or laser-based consolidation.
generation.conditions: Perform transient liquid‐phase sintering or rapid laser consolidation under an inert or vacuum atmosphere at temperatures high enough to melt copper (e.g., around 1100–1200 °C) but well below tungsten’s melting point. Service testing should mimic fusion reactor joint conditions including moderate thermal loads (<700 °C) and irradiation exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: The nickel coating promotes the formation of a thin interfacial intermetallic layer between tungsten and copper, which lowers the interfacial tension and enhances liquid metal infiltration. This mediator minimizes the formation of voids and suppresses phase segregation between the constituents.
generation.mechanism: Nickel acts as an active wetting agent that reduces the surface energy difference between molten copper and refractory tungsten. This modification facilitates uniform wetting of tungsten surfaces during processing, leading to improved bonding and reduced porosity, which ultimately enhances thermal transport and mechanical durability under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional W–Cu composites that show significant void fractions and phase separation, the Ni-coated composite is predicted to exhibit a denser microstructure, lower void volume fraction, higher effective thermal conductivity, and improved mechanical durability under simulated fusion-relevant irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composites fabricated by conventional spark plasma sintering or metal 3D printing without any interfacial treatment, which typically suffer from poor wetting, phase separation, and void formation.
generation.boundary: The processing window is limited to temperature regimes sufficient for melting copper (approximately 1100–1200 °C) yet below copper’s boiling point, with service conditions reflecting fusion reactor joint environments (moderate operating temperatures and irradiation doses). The intervention’s effectiveness and stability under extended irradiation and thermal cycling remain to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal nickel coating thickness and its long-term behavior under high-dose irradiation and thermal cycling are not fully established, and there may be uncertainties related to potential intermetallic formation that could affect mechanical durability over very long service times.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites under identical processing conditions: one using tungsten particles pre-coated with a 50–100 nm nickel layer and a control set with uncoated tungsten particles. Use transient liquid-phase sintering or laser consolidation at ~1100–1200 °C. Characterize the resulting microstructures using SEM/TEM and measure density (e.g., by Archimedes method). Perform thermal conductivity tests and mechanical durability assessments (e.g., hardness, fracture toughness). Subject samples to simulated irradiation conditions representative of fusion reactor joint environments.
measurements: Void volume fraction and pore distribution from SEM/TEM imaging
Microstructural stability before and after irradiation exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., lower porosity, higher density and thermal conductivity, and better retention of mechanical properties under irradiation) compared to the control samples, the hypothesis is rejected.
